children.text: Common Signs and Symptoms of Depression

Depression can affect emotions, thoughts, physical health, behavior, relationships, and everyday functioning. Although persistent sadness is commonly associated with depression, it is only one possible symptom.

Some people feel empty, irritable, restless, disconnected, or emotionally numb rather than visibly sad. Others first notice exhaustion, poor concentration, sleep problems, appetite changes, unexplained physical discomfort, or loss of interest in activities that once mattered to them.

Depression does not look the same in every person. Symptoms may differ in number, intensity, duration, and effect on daily life. A person may experience several symptoms at once or have a smaller number of symptoms that still cause significant distress or impairment.

The National Institute of Mental Health identifies emotional, cognitive, behavioral, physical, and safety-related changes among the common signs of depression. A person does not need to experience every symptom to deserve an evaluation.
This page explains the common signs and symptoms of depression. It does not provide a diagnosis. For a foundational explanation of the condition, visit
Depression Symptoms Can Affect Several Areas at Once
Depression is not defined by one isolated feeling or behavior.
A person may have a combination of changes involving:

For example, someone may stop enjoying time with friends, begin sleeping much longer, struggle to concentrate at work, feel guilty about falling behind, and withdraw because they believe they are disappointing everyone.
Another person may become irritable, restless, unable to sleep, physically uncomfortable, and increasingly dependent on alcohol without describing themselves as sad.
The pattern, persistence, severity, and effect on functioning are more important than any one symptom.
Persistent sadness is one of the most recognized symptoms of depression.
The sadness may be present for much of the day and continue across many days.
It may occur after a loss, relationship difficulty, health concern, work problem, financial stress, or another painful event. It may also appear without one clearly identifiable cause.

Ordinary sadness can be intense, but it often changes with time, circumstances, comfort, or positive experiences. Depression may be more persistent and may occur together with loss of pleasure, low energy, sleep disturbance, guilt, poor concentration, or functional decline.
A person should not dismiss persistent sadness simply because other people believe there is no reason for it.
Not everyone with depression feels noticeably sad.
Feeling as though they are moving through life automatically
A person may understand intellectually that an event is important while experiencing little emotional reaction.
They may attend a celebration, spend time with family, achieve something meaningful, or receive positive news without feeling the emotional response they expected.
Emotional numbness can be distressing because the person may fear they no longer care about people or activities that once mattered deeply.
Loss of interest or pleasure is called anhedonia.
It may involve reduced interest in:
A person may stop participating entirely or continue the activity without feeling enjoyment.
“I do not look forward to anything.”
“I still go, but I feel absent.”
“I cannot remember the last time I enjoyed myself.”
Depressed mood and loss of interest are central symptoms clinicians consider when evaluating major depression.
Loss of interest should not automatically be interpreted as laziness, ingratitude, or rejection of other people.
Depression can affect how a person views the future.
The person may interpret temporary problems as permanent and ordinary setbacks as proof that improvement is impossible.
Hopelessness may lead someone to stop:
Hopelessness deserves particular attention because it may occur alongside thoughts of death or suicide.
Depression can appear as irritability rather than sadness.
Avoid people because interaction feels exhausting
Feel overwhelmed by noise or demands
This may be especially noticeable to family members, coworkers, or classmates.
A person may feel guilty afterward and wonder why they are reacting differently from their usual self.

Irritability can occur with several mental health and medical concerns, including depression, anxiety, trauma-related conditions, sleep deprivation, substance use, medication effects, and bipolar disorder. It should be considered within the full symptom pattern.
NIMH includes irritability, frustration, anger, and restlessness among changes that may occur with depression.
Depression may produce guilt that is excessive, persistent, or disconnected from the actual situation.
A person may feel guilty about:
Being unable to complete household tasks
The guilt may continue even after reassurance or reasonable efforts to correct a problem.

A parent may believe they have failed their children because they are struggling with energy. An employee may view one mistake as proof that they are incompetent. A student may believe falling behind means they have ruined their entire future.
Guilt becomes especially concerning when the person believes they deserve punishment or that other people would be better without them.
Depression can affect a person’s sense of value and identity.
“My family would be better without me.”
These beliefs may feel completely convincing during depression.
Worthlessness differs from acknowledging a specific mistake. It involves a broad negative judgment about the entire person.
Persistent worthlessness should be discussed with a mental health professional, particularly when it occurs with hopelessness, self-harm, or suicidal thinking.
A person with depression may feel unable to influence their circumstances.
This feeling can reduce help-seeking and increase avoidance.
The person may know that contacting a provider, opening a bill, attending class, or asking for support would be useful but feel unable to begin.
Helplessness is not necessarily unwillingness. Depression may interfere with the motivation, planning, energy, and hope required to act.
Fatigue is a common and often disabling symptom of depression.
Having no energy after work or school
Feeling exhausted despite sleeping for many hours
Routine activities may feel unusually demanding.
Showering may feel like a major project
Preparing food may feel too complicated
Answering a message may require significant effort
Walking from one room to another may feel exhausting

Fatigue can also result from sleep disorders, anemia, thyroid conditions, chronic illness, medication effects, pain, infection, or other medical concerns. Persistent or unexplained fatigue may require both psychiatric and medical evaluation.
Depression may cause noticeable slowing in movement, speech, and thinking.
Speak quietly or with long pauses
Sit in one position for long periods
Feel that their body is unusually heavy
Need more time to complete ordinary tasks
Feel as though their thoughts are moving through thick fog
Clinicians may refer to significant slowing as psychomotor retardation.
The American Psychiatric Association includes observable slowing of movement or speech among symptoms that may occur in major depression.
Severe slowing, confusion, inability to speak normally, sudden weakness, or other abrupt neurological changes require medical attention rather than being assumed to result from depression.
Depression does not always cause slowing.
Some people become physically restless or agitated.
Feel emotionally distressed and physically activated
This can be particularly uncomfortable when the person also feels hopeless or suicidal.
Restlessness may also be related to anxiety, medication side effects, substance use, withdrawal, mania, mixed mood symptoms, or medical conditions.
New severe restlessness after starting or changing medication should be reported promptly to the prescribing professional.
Depression may interfere with the ability to focus and sustain attention.
Need much longer to complete familiar work
Someone who normally considers themselves capable may become frightened by this change.
They may think they are becoming unintelligent or permanently unable to function.

Concentration problems can occur with depression, but they may also be related to anxiety, ADHD, sleep loss, medication effects, substance use, pain, or medical illness. A clinical evaluation considers the broader pattern.
Depression may affect short-term memory or the ability to recall recently presented information.
Sometimes the problem begins with concentration. Information that was not fully processed may be difficult to recall later.
New, severe, or rapidly worsening memory problems should receive medical attention, especially when accompanied by confusion, speech changes, weakness, head injury, fever, or other physical symptoms.
Ordinary decisions may become overwhelming during depression.
A person may struggle to choose:
How to solve a basic problem
How to respond to a work request
The person may postpone decisions because every option feels wrong.
When possible, it may be helpful to delay major irreversible decisions during severe depression and discuss them with a trusted person or qualified professional.
Depression may affect sleep in several ways.
Staying in bed throughout the day
Some people experience insomnia. Others experience excessive sleep.
Sleep symptoms may worsen energy, concentration, mood, and physical wellbeing.

It is important to report any history of sleeping very little while remaining unusually energized. Reduced need for sleep with increased activity, racing thoughts, rapid speech, confidence, irritability, or impulsivity may indicate mania, hypomania, medication activation, substance effects, or another condition rather than depression alone.
NIMH lists insomnia, early-morning waking, and oversleeping among common depression symptoms.
Depression may reduce or increase appetite.
Feel that food has no taste
Appetite changes may lead to unintended weight loss or gain.
The person may also have difficulty shopping, cooking, or cleaning even when hunger remains normal.

Appetite and weight changes can have many causes, including medication, medical illness, hormonal changes, eating disorders, stress, and substance use. Significant or unexplained changes deserve professional evaluation.
Depression-related changes in appetite, activity, and routine may contribute to weight loss or gain.
A person may lose weight because they:
A person may gain weight because they:
Weight alone does not diagnose depression.
Rapid or medically concerning weight changes should be evaluated because physical illness, medication effects, hormonal conditions, and other concerns may be involved.
Depression may occur with physical symptoms such as:
Some people seek care for physical discomfort before recognizing changes in mood or interest.
Physical pain is not imaginary simply because depression may be present.
New, severe, persistent, or unexplained symptoms should be medically evaluated. Depression can occur alongside physical illness, and medical conditions may also cause depression-like symptoms.
NIMH includes persistent aches, headaches, cramps, and digestive concerns without a clear physical explanation among symptoms that can accompany depression.
A feeling of heaviness after eating
Digestive symptoms can also result from medication, anxiety, infection, food intolerance, gastrointestinal conditions, or other medical issues.
A healthcare professional may need to evaluate both emotional and physical factors.
Depression may affect sexual interest, arousal, emotional intimacy, and body confidence.
Become concerned about disappointing a partner
Medication, hormonal changes, relationship stress, physical illness, and other factors may also affect sexual functioning.
Patients should feel able to discuss sexual concerns with a healthcare professional. These symptoms can affect quality of life and treatment participation.
Do not stop medication abruptly because of sexual side effects. Discuss concerns with the prescribing professional.
A person with depression may begin avoiding other people.
Stop attending religious or community activities
Believing no one wants them around
Withdrawal may be misunderstood as rejection or lack of care.
A person may still value the relationship but feel unable to participate in it.
Depression may change how often and how clearly someone communicates.
Feel they have nothing worth saying
This can create distance in relationships and make it harder for others to recognize worsening symptoms.
These changes may result from low energy, reduced motivation, poor concentration, or a feeling that self-care no longer matters.
A major decline in hygiene may indicate increasing severity or functional impairment.
It should be approached with concern rather than shame.
The person may repeatedly promise themselves they will begin later but remain unable to act.
Responsibilities can accumulate and increase guilt, anxiety, and hopelessness.
Feeling unable to tolerate ordinary pressure
Some people continue performing while experiencing significant hidden distress.
The ability to remain employed does not rule out serious depression or suicide risk.
A previously engaged student may appear uninterested or careless when they are actually experiencing significant depressive symptoms.
Some people use alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, or other substances to manage:
Substance use can worsen sleep, judgment, medication safety, and mood. It can also make diagnosis more difficult.
Honest disclosure helps the clinician understand the complete pattern.
Although withdrawal and reduced activity are common, some people with depression may engage in risky behavior.
Risk-taking may reflect hopelessness, reduced concern for personal safety, substance use, agitation, bipolar disorder, or another condition.
NIMH notes that some people with depression may become more involved in high-risk activities.
A sudden major behavioral change deserves professional attention.
Depression may involve thoughts such as:
“I wish I would not wake up.”
“It would be easier if I were gone.”
“I do not care what happens to me.”
A person may think about death without having a specific suicide plan. These thoughts are still clinically important and should be discussed directly with a healthcare professional.
Do not minimize passive thoughts of death because the person says they would never act. Risk can change, and professional assessment may be needed.
Saying others would be better without them
Suicidal statements and behavior should always be taken seriously.
Do not promise to keep a suicide plan secret.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone has attempted suicide, intends to act, has access to lethal means, has taken an overdose, or cannot remain safe.
Severe depression may sometimes occur with psychotic symptoms.
Seeing things others do not see
Believing something that is clearly disconnected from reality
Believing they have caused a disaster
Believing they have committed an unforgivable act
Believing they have lost everything despite evidence otherwise
Depression with psychotic features requires prompt professional evaluation and may carry increased suicide risk.
Psychosis can also occur with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia-spectrum conditions, substance use, medication reactions, neurological illness, and other medical concerns.
Severe psychosis, dangerous behavior, or inability to remain safe requires emergency care.
Symptoms May Be Mild, Moderate, or Severe
Depression exists across a range of severity.
A person may continue functioning but notice:
Inability to eat or drink adequately
The number of symptoms does not tell the entire story. Their intensity, duration, functional effect, and safety implications also matter.
At the same time, they may experience:
Inability to function outside public responsibilities
The informal phrase “high-functioning depression” is sometimes used to describe people who appear to maintain daily routines while privately struggling, but it is not a formal diagnosis.
Statements such as “You do not look depressed” may discourage disclosure.
Children may not describe depression in adult language.
Behavioral changes should be considered within the child’s developmental stage, family situation, school environment, health, and overall functioning.
Ordinary sadness, frustration, or developmental behavior should not automatically be labeled as depression.
Persistent or concerning changes deserve evaluation.
Loss of interest in friends or activities
A teenager may appear defiant or unmotivated while experiencing significant emotional distress.
Statements about death, self-harm, or having no reason to live should never be dismissed as drama or attention-seeking.
Older adults may be more likely to report:
Depression should not be considered a normal part of aging.
New depressive, cognitive, or behavioral symptoms later in life may require review of:
Sudden confusion or abrupt behavioral change requires medical attention.
Depression During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
Depression can occur during pregnancy and after delivery.
Sleep problems beyond expected infant disruption
A parent can love their baby and still experience depression.
Severe confusion, hallucinations, delusions, dangerous behavior, or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby may indicate an emergency and require immediate care.
Depression Symptoms May Follow a Seasonal Pattern
Some people experience depressive symptoms during a particular season.
A recurring seasonal pattern may require evaluation for seasonal affective disorder.
It is more than simply disliking winter, cold weather, or shorter days.
Signs That May Point to Bipolar Depression
A depressive episode may occur as part of bipolar disorder.
Tell the evaluating professional about any previous periods involving:
A noticeable change after starting an antidepressant
A person may seek care during depression and not initially recognize a previous hypomanic period as clinically relevant.
The distinction matters because treatment recommendations may differ.
Symptoms That May Have Another Cause
Certain medicines and medical conditions may produce symptoms that resemble depression.
A comprehensive evaluation helps determine whether depression, another condition, or several contributing concerns may be present.
A Symptom List Cannot Diagnose Depression
Online symptom lists can help people recognize concerns, but they cannot confirm a diagnosis.
Whether they represent a change from usual functioning
Whether mania or hypomania has occurred
Whether substances or medications may be involved
Whether a medical condition may contribute
Screening questionnaires can support an evaluation, but they do not replace clinical assessment.
Consider seeking a professional evaluation when symptoms:
Continue for approximately two weeks or longer
Include thoughts of death or suicide
NIMH recommends seeking professional help when severe or distressing symptoms persist or interfere with daily activities.
Do not wait two weeks when symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening, medically dangerous, or affecting safety.
When to Seek Help for Depression.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
May harm themselves or another person
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Is placing children or vulnerable people at risk
A routine appointment request, website form, email, voicemail, or portal message should not replace emergency care.
How Tinka Health Services Can Help

Tinka Health Services provides psychiatric evaluation, depression assessment, therapy-informed support, medication management when clinically appropriate, and telehealth mental health care for eligible patients in Maryland, Washington, DC, and Virginia.
Seliat Dosunmu, DNP, PMHNP-BC, FNP-C, works with patients to understand the full pattern of symptoms and how those symptoms affect everyday life.

An appointment does not guarantee a depression diagnosis, medication prescription, or specific treatment. Recommendations depend on the clinical evaluation, medical history, functional needs, treatment history, preferences, and safety concerns.
Telehealth appointments may be available for eligible patients physically located in Maryland, Washington, DC, or Virginia when virtual care is clinically appropriate.
Tinka Health Services is not an emergency service. For non-emergency psychiatric care, visit
When to Seek Help for Depression
Common signs and symptoms of depression may affect mood, interest, energy, sleep, appetite, concentration, memory, movement, physical wellbeing, behavior, relationships, and daily functioning.

A person may feel sad, empty, hopeless, irritable, guilty, worthless, exhausted, restless, slowed down, or emotionally numb. They may stop enjoying activities, withdraw from other people, neglect personal care, struggle at work or school, experience appetite or sleep changes, or develop unexplained physical discomfort.

Depression does not look the same in everyone. Some people remain outwardly functional while experiencing severe hidden distress. Children, teenagers, older adults, pregnant or postpartum patients, and people with medical conditions may also show different symptom patterns.

A symptom list cannot diagnose depression. Professional evaluation considers duration, severity, functional effect, medical history, medication or substance use, possible mania or hypomania, and current safety.

Persistent or functionally impairing symptoms deserve professional attention. Suicidal behavior, overdose, severe psychosis, inability to meet basic needs, or inability to remain safe requires immediate emergency care.

children.text: How Depression Can Affect Daily Functioning

Depression can interfere with the practical abilities a person uses to manage everyday life. It may affect getting out of bed, preparing meals, maintaining hygiene, concentrating, making decisions, completing work, attending school, managing money, caring for children, communicating with others, and following medical recommendations.
These difficulties are known as functional impairment.

Functional impairment does not mean that a person has lost every ability or responsibility. Someone may continue working, parenting, studying, or attending appointments while finding each activity much harder than usual. Another person may experience a more severe decline and become unable to meet basic needs without support.

Depression can affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities such as sleeping, eating, and working. Major depression may cause severe impairment that limits a person’s ability to carry out important life activities.

Difficulty functioning during depression is not necessarily laziness, carelessness, lack of intelligence, or unwillingness to try. Depression can interfere with energy, motivation, concentration, memory, planning, decision-making, movement, emotional connection, and the ability to anticipate that effort will lead to a meaningful result.
This page focuses specifically on functional impairment. For a broader discussion of how depression may shape routines and personal experiences, visit
Functional impairment means that symptoms make it harder for a person to perform expected activities or fulfill important roles.
Clinicians may consider functioning in areas such as:
The level of impairment can range from mild to severe.
A person with mild impairment may continue meeting responsibilities but require more time, effort, reminders, or recovery afterward.
A person with moderate impairment may begin missing work, falling behind at school, avoiding relationships, neglecting household tasks, or struggling with self-care.
Severe impairment may involve an inability to work, study, eat adequately, maintain hygiene, care for dependents, manage medication, or remain safe.
SAMHSA describes depression as a condition that can inhibit daily functioning and interfere with activities that normally provide pleasure.
Why Depression Can Make Simple Tasks Feel Difficult
Many ordinary activities involve several mental and physical steps.
Taking a shower may require a person to:
Recognize that the task needs to be done
When depression affects energy, task initiation, concentration, movement, and motivation, this sequence may feel overwhelming.
The same problem may occur with:
Someone may know exactly what needs to happen and still feel unable to begin.
This difference between knowing and doing is one of the most frustrating aspects of depression-related functional impairment.
Task initiation is the ability to begin an activity.
A person with depression may repeatedly think:
Despite understanding the need, they may remain unable to act.
This can occur because depression affects:
Hope that the effort will matter
A delayed task may then create guilt, shame, or practical consequences. Those consequences make the task feel larger and may lead to further avoidance.
A person delays opening a bill.
The person feels ashamed and afraid to look.
Practical support may focus on beginning one small step rather than completing the entire task at once.
Starting an activity does not always mean the person can complete it.
Begin several tasks but lose energy
Believe the work is not good enough
Abandon the task because completion feels pointless
A person might begin washing dishes and stop after two items. They may open a work document but be unable to organize their thoughts. They may begin cooking and lose track of the steps.
This can create a home or work environment filled with unfinished responsibilities, which may increase anxiety and self-criticism.
Low energy can significantly limit functioning.
They may use most of their energy on one essential responsibility.
For example, someone may complete a workday but be unable to prepare food, talk with family, clean, or attend to personal care afterward.
Another person may care for their children but neglect their own meals, medical appointments, or sleep.
Outward functioning may therefore hide the extent of impairment.
Motivation involves more than deciding that something is important.
It also depends on the ability to anticipate a benefit, begin an action, maintain effort, and believe that completion is possible.
Depression may reduce the expectation that an activity will feel rewarding.
This may affect activities the person genuinely values, including:
The loss of motivation does not prove that the person no longer cares.
Concentration difficulties can interfere with nearly every area of functioning.
Become overwhelmed by several pieces of information
Need much longer to complete familiar work
At work, this may appear as reduced productivity or poor performance.
At school, it may appear as falling grades, missed assignments, or lack of participation.
At home, the person may forget what they intended to do, leave appliances on, lose items, or overlook important responsibilities.
Depression commonly affects concentration and decision-making, and these changes can contribute to difficulty completing normal tasks.
Depression may affect the ability to remember recent information.
Sometimes the information was not fully processed because concentration was reduced.

New, severe, or rapidly worsening memory problems should not automatically be attributed to depression. Medical, neurological, sleep-related, medication-related, and substance-related causes may also need to be considered.
Depression may make ordinary choices feel difficult.
A person may struggle to decide:
How to respond to a family concern
Whether to continue a course or job
Negative thinking may also influence major decisions.
They are incapable of making a good choice
Others would be better without them
There is no reason to preserve opportunities
When possible, major irreversible decisions may deserve additional time and discussion during a severe depressive period.
This does not mean that every decision made while depressed is invalid. It means that depression may narrow the person’s view of available options.
Depression can affect the ability to estimate time, prioritize tasks, maintain schedules, and transition between activities.
Lose track of time in bed
Spend hours trying to begin one task
Become unable to decide what should happen first
Avoid a schedule because it feels overwhelming
Work slowly and fall further behind
The person may appear disorganized even when they previously managed time effectively.
Depression may affect bathing, oral care, grooming, laundry, and clothing changes.
Feel unable to maintain their appearance
A decline in hygiene should be approached with concern rather than shame.
Severe self-neglect may indicate that depression is becoming more serious.
Functional impairment may affect shopping, meal planning, cooking, eating, and cleaning afterward.
Leave dishes or spoiled food unattended
Someone may have a normal appetite but still be unable to complete the practical steps needed to prepare food.
A person who cannot eat or drink adequately, is becoming physically weak, or cannot meet basic nutritional needs may require urgent medical care.
Sleep changes can affect daytime functioning even when the person spends many hours in bed.
Poor sleep may make it harder to:
Sleeping for many hours does not always restore energy during depression.
A history of sleeping very little while feeling unusually energized should be reported because it may suggest mania, hypomania, medication activation, substance effects, or another condition.
As unfinished tasks accumulate, the person may become ashamed and avoid asking for help.
They may stop inviting others into the home or fear being judged.
A practical approach may begin with safety rather than appearance.
Ensuring that dependents and pets are cared for
The goal is not immediate perfection. It is restoring a manageable and safe environment.
Depression may affect attendance, productivity, judgment, communication, and confidence.
A person may continue working while experiencing significant impairment.
They may use all their available energy to perform at work and then become unable to function at home.
Depression-related work difficulties can create a cycle:
The person becomes anxious and ashamed.
Fear of job loss increases depression.
A gradual return after an absence
Workplace, disability, or legal questions should be discussed with appropriate qualified resources.
Students experiencing depression may struggle with:
A student may spend hours looking at an assignment without knowing how to begin.
They may stop checking email, avoid instructors, or believe falling behind means their future is permanently ruined.
A major decline in attendance, grades, behavior, or social engagement deserves attention.
Depression can interfere with communication, emotional responsiveness, intimacy, patience, and social participation.
Family members or friends may interpret withdrawal as rejection.
The person may care deeply about the relationship but feel unable to participate.
“I am experiencing depression and may respond slowly. My withdrawal is not because I do not care.”
Asking directly about safety when concerned
Social interaction may require energy, concentration, emotional responsiveness, and confidence.
Depression may make conversation feel exhausting.
Believe they have nothing to contribute
Social withdrawal may provide temporary relief from demands but increase loneliness and hopelessness.
Reconnection may begin with small steps, such as:
Sitting quietly with a trusted person
Asking someone to accompany them to an appointment
Depression may affect a parent’s energy, patience, attention, organization, and emotional availability.
Having depression does not mean a person does not love their children or cannot parent effectively.
A written plan for severe episodes
Children may benefit from a simple, age-appropriate explanation that the parent is receiving help and that the condition is not the child’s fault.
When depression prevents a parent from meeting a child’s essential safety or care needs, additional support should be arranged promptly.
A person caring for children, older adults, a partner, or another relative may experience depression while continuing to carry significant responsibilities.
Caregivers may avoid seeking help because they believe no one else can take over.
Seeking support may protect both the caregiver and the person who depends on them.
Depression may affect money management through avoidance, concentration problems, low energy, reduced income, or hopelessness.
Feel unable to ask for assistance
Financial problems may then increase depressive symptoms.
A short list of urgent financial tasks
Qualified financial or legal guidance when necessary
The person should remain involved in decisions whenever possible.
A person should not drive when symptoms, medication effects, alcohol, substances, exhaustion, or suicidal thinking make driving unsafe.
Using a vehicle during a suicide plan
Immediate safety concerns require urgent or emergency intervention.
Depression can make it harder to manage physical-health conditions.
Stop monitoring blood sugar or blood pressure
Feel unable to follow treatment recommendations
Depression frequently occurs alongside chronic medical conditions, and it may increase the difficulty of managing those illnesses.
Mental and physical healthcare may need to be coordinated.
A new medical symptom should not automatically be attributed to depression.
Depression may interfere with taking both psychiatric and medical medication.
Lose track of whether medication was taken
Use alcohol or substances with prescriptions
Medication should not be stopped, restarted, increased, decreased, or doubled without professional guidance.
Possible overdose or intentional misuse requires emergency help.
Some people with depression move, speak, and think more slowly.
Take much longer to complete tasks
Others may experience agitation and restlessness.
Either slowing or agitation can interfere with work, sleep, relationships, and self-care.
New severe restlessness may also be a medication side effect or a sign of anxiety, substance use, withdrawal, mixed symptoms, or another condition.
Depression may affect the ability to explain needs, answer questions, or participate in conversations.
Forget what they intended to say
Feel unable to ask for help
Hide symptoms to avoid burdening people
This can make treatment more difficult if the clinician does not receive an accurate picture.
Writing notes before an appointment may help the patient explain:
What they can no longer manage
A person who misses work, forgets information, or struggles with hygiene may begin to believe:
Treatment may need to address both the depressive symptoms and the practical consequences that developed while functioning was impaired.
Functional impairment is not always visible.
Become unable to complete basic tasks
Public performance does not necessarily reflect private functioning.
A person who appears successful may still need professional help.
Functional Impairment May Change From Day to Day
A person may complete several tasks one day and struggle to get out of bed the next.
This does not mean that the impairment is imaginary or that the person could function normally at all times if they tried harder.
A better day does not automatically mean the depression has resolved.
Functional Impairment in Children and Teenagers
Younger people may show impairment through:
A teenager may appear defiant or careless when concentration, motivation, hope, and sleep have been affected.
Statements about death, self-harm, or having no reason to live should never be dismissed as drama.
Depression is not a normal part of aging.
New functional decline later in life may require assessment for:
Sudden confusion or abrupt loss of functioning requires medical attention.
Functional Impairment During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
Depression during pregnancy or after delivery may affect:
A person may love their baby and still experience severe impairment.
Family or practical support may be especially important for:
Severe confusion, hallucinations, unusual beliefs, dangerous behavior, or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby require emergency care.
Depressive episodes can occur in both major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.
Patients should report any history of:
Treatment recommendations may differ when depression occurs as part of bipolar disorder.
A mental health professional may ask:
How much effort does functioning require?
Are you attending work or school?
Are you caring safely for children or dependents?
Are bills and essential tasks being managed?

The clinician may consider functioning at home, at work or school, in relationships, and in social life. Measures used in depression research and assessment also examine how symptoms interfere with major life roles.
Screening questionnaires may support the evaluation but do not replace a clinical assessment.
How Improvement in Functioning May Appear
Functional recovery may begin before the person feels completely well.
Getting out of bed more consistently
Returning to work for limited hours
Progress may be gradual and uneven.
Someone may begin eating and sleeping more regularly while still struggling with concentration. Another person may return to work but continue needing help at home.
Treatment progress should consider symptoms, functioning, physical health, quality of life, and safety.
Practical strategies may support daily life but should not be treated as a replacement for professional care.
Instead of “clean the house,” begin with:
Keep daily items in the same place
“Can you drive me to the appointment?”
“Can you help me call the office?”
“Can you sit with me while I open the mail?”
“Can you help with childcare this afternoon?”
What Family and Friends Can Do
Asking directly about suicide when concerned
“I have noticed that you have missed work, stopped eating regularly, and are staying in bed most of the day. I am concerned and would like to help you contact a professional.”
“You have nothing to be depressed about.”
Criticism may increase shame and withdrawal.
When Functional Impairment Deserves Professional Attention
Consider seeking a professional evaluation when depression makes it difficult to:
A person does not need to be completely unable to function before requesting help.
NIMH encourages people to consider how mental health symptoms affect daily life and to contact a healthcare professional when symptoms worsen or do not improve.
When to Seek Help for Depression.
When Urgent Help May Be Needed
Prompt or urgent evaluation may be needed when someone:
Is rapidly losing the ability to function
Has stopped eating or drinking adequately
Cannot care safely for children or dependents
Is using increasing amounts of alcohol or substances
Has thoughts of death or suicide
The appropriate next step may involve an earlier psychiatric appointment, urgent care, crisis assessment, medical evaluation, or emergency services.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
May harm themselves or another person
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Is placing children or vulnerable people at risk
Severe depression may become life-threatening when a person stops eating or drinking or faces a high risk of suicide.
Do not rely on a routine appointment request, website form, voicemail, email, or patient portal during an immediate emergency.
Common Misconceptions About Depression and Functioning
“A Person Who Can Work Is Functioning Normally”
Someone may maintain employment while experiencing severe impairment at home, in relationships, or in personal care.
“If They Completed One Task, They Can Complete Everything”
Tasks require different amounts of concentration, planning, energy, emotional effort, and time.
Depression may impair motivation, task initiation, concentration, and expectation of reward.
“Staying in Bed Means the Person Is Resting”
A person may remain in bed because of exhaustion, hopelessness, slowed movement, avoidance, or sleep disruption without feeling restored.
“A Messy Home Means the Person Does Not Care”
Depression may interfere with organization, decision-making, energy, and follow-through.
Criticism and shame may worsen avoidance. Clear, manageable support is often more useful.
Routines may support functioning, but they do not replace professional assessment and treatment when symptoms are persistent, severe, recurring, or dangerous.
How Tinka Health Services Can Help

Tinka Health Services provides psychiatric evaluation, depression assessment, therapy-informed support, medication management when clinically appropriate, and telehealth mental health care for eligible patients in Maryland, Washington, DC, and Virginia.
A depression evaluation may include discussion of how symptoms affect:
Seliat Dosunmu, DNP, PMHNP-BC, FNP-C, works with patients to understand both the depressive symptoms and the practical ways those symptoms are affecting daily life.
Depending on the clinical evaluation, recommendations may include:
Coordination with therapists or medical professionals
A higher level of care when needed

An appointment does not guarantee a depression diagnosis, medication prescription, or specific treatment. Recommendations depend on symptoms, medical history, previous care, current functioning, preferences, and safety needs.
Telehealth appointments may be available for eligible patients physically located in Maryland, Washington, DC, or Virginia when virtual care is clinically appropriate.
Tinka Health Services is not an emergency service. For non-emergency psychiatric care, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Depression
When to Seek Help for Depression

Depression can affect the practical abilities needed to manage everyday life, including task initiation, concentration, memory, decision-making, personal hygiene, eating, sleep, work, school, relationships, parenting, finances, household responsibilities, and medical care.

A person may understand exactly what needs to be done and still struggle to begin or complete it. These difficulties may reflect changes in energy, motivation, concentration, movement, planning, self-confidence, and hope rather than laziness or lack of concern.
Functional impairment may be visible or hidden. Some people become unable to meet basic responsibilities, while others continue working or caring for family at significant personal cost.

Practical strategies such as reducing tasks, limiting decisions, using reminders, requesting specific help, and prioritizing essential needs may support functioning. They do not replace professional care when symptoms are persistent, recurring, severe, or dangerous.

A significant decline in self-care, eating, drinking, work, school, parenting, medical treatment, or safety should be taken seriously. Suicidal behavior, overdose, severe psychosis, inability to meet basic needs, or inability to remain safe requires immediate emergency care.

children.text: Depression warning signs are changes in mood, thinking, behavior, physical wellbeing, or daily functioning that may indicate depression is developing, returning, or becoming more severe.

Some warning signs are easy to recognize, such as persistent sadness, frequent crying, or statements about hopelessness. Others may be less obvious. A person may become irritable, stop answering messages, neglect personal care, sleep throughout the day, miss work, use more alcohol, or seem emotionally disconnected.
Warning signs do not look the same in everyone. Some people become visibly distressed, while others continue working, parenting, studying, or socializing despite significant internal suffering.
A single change does not automatically mean someone has depression. Warning signs become more concerning when they:
Represent a clear change from usual functioning
Follow a painful event, loss, or major life change
Include thoughts of death, suicide, or self-harm

The National Institute of Mental Health identifies persistent low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness, irritability, fatigue, sleep or appetite changes, concentration problems, social withdrawal, increased substance use, inability to meet responsibilities, and thoughts of death or suicide among signs that may occur with depression.
Recognizing warning signs early may help someone seek care before symptoms lead to severe functional decline or an immediate safety crisis.
This page focuses on changes that may signal emerging or worsening depression. For a detailed explanation of individual symptoms, visit
Common Signs and Symptoms of Depression.
What Is the Difference Between a Symptom and a Warning Sign?
A symptom is an experience that may be part of depression, such as low mood, fatigue, poor concentration, or loss of interest.
A warning sign is a symptom or change that suggests the condition may be beginning, returning, worsening, or becoming unsafe.
Difficulty sleeping may be a symptom of depression.
Sleeping poorly for several nights and then becoming increasingly hopeless may be a warning that depression is worsening.
Social withdrawal may be a symptom.
Suddenly ending contact with close friends and giving away important belongings may be a serious safety warning sign.
Low energy may be a symptom.
Becoming unable to eat, bathe, attend work, or care for children may signal severe functional decline.
The same behavior can have different meanings depending on the person’s usual habits, the surrounding circumstances, and the other changes occurring at the same time.
Warning Signs Often Involve a Change From Normal Functioning
What is different from this person’s usual behavior?
Are several areas of life being affected?
Has this pattern occurred before a depressive episode?
Someone who has always preferred limited social contact may not be showing a warning sign simply because they spend time alone.
However, a normally engaged person who suddenly stops responding, misses work, remains in bed, and says nothing matters may be experiencing a significant change.
Personal patterns are especially important for people who have experienced previous depressive episodes.
One person’s earliest warning sign may be sleeping longer. Another may stop cooking, withdraw from a partner, become unusually irritable, or begin missing medical appointments.
Feeling unable to look forward to anything
A person may describe the change by saying:
These changes may deserve attention even before the person meets full criteria for a depressive disorder.
Loss of Interest as a Warning Sign
A loss of interest or pleasure may be one of the earliest signs that depression is returning.
The change may initially seem minor.
Someone may skip one activity, then stop participating altogether. Another may continue attending but feel emotionally absent.
Family members may notice that the person no longer talks about interests that were previously important.
Statements such as the following may be warning signs:
“I do not care whether I go.”
“There is nothing to look forward to.”
Hopelessness is a significant depression warning sign.
A person may begin believing that:
The future has been permanently damaged
They will always feel this way
Their family would be better without them
Hopelessness may cause the person to stop trying to address problems, attend treatment, complete responsibilities, or maintain relationships.
It becomes especially concerning when accompanied by:
NIMH lists feeling empty, hopeless, trapped, or without a reason to live among warning signs that may indicate suicide risk.
Depression may appear as irritability, frustration, anger, or reduced patience.
Becoming overwhelmed by noise or requests
Irritability can occur with several conditions, including anxiety, trauma-related concerns, substance use, sleep deprivation, medication effects, and bipolar disorder.
Irritability combined with low energy, withdrawal, hopelessness, sleep changes, loss of interest, or declining functioning may indicate depression.
Some people do not become visibly sad when depression develops.
Instead, they may become emotionally numb.
Showing little reaction to good or bad news
Describing life as unreal or distant
Losing interest in relationships or goals
Emotional numbness can be mistaken for calmness, indifference, or lack of concern.
A person may still care deeply but feel unable to experience or express that connection.
Depression may cause guilt or shame to become excessive and difficult to challenge.
The person may repeatedly apologize for:
They may view one problem as proof that they are a complete failure.
Statements such as the following deserve attention:
“My family should not have to deal with me.”
Great guilt, shame, and feeling like a burden are also recognized suicide warning signs.
Depression may change the way a person thinks, remembers, and makes decisions.
Becoming unable to make simple decisions
The person may begin falling behind before recognizing that depression is involved.
They may interpret concentration problems as proof that they are incapable, which can deepen shame and avoidance.
New severe confusion, sudden memory loss, speech changes, weakness, or other neurological symptoms require medical evaluation rather than being assumed to result from depression.
Sleep changes may appear before other symptoms become obvious.
Remaining in bed during the day
Depending on alcohol, cannabis, or nonprescribed products to sleep
Family members may notice that the person is no longer following their usual schedule.
Sleep changes should be evaluated within the full pattern.

A history of sleeping very little while feeling unusually energized, confident, talkative, active, or impulsive should be reported. That pattern may suggest mania, hypomania, medication activation, substance effects, or another condition rather than depression alone.
Changes in appetite or weight may signal worsening depression.
Eat more frequently for emotional relief
A person may have an appetite but still be unable to complete the steps required to shop, cook, eat, and clean.
Significant appetite or weight changes should be evaluated because medication effects, medical illness, hormonal conditions, eating disorders, and substance use may also contribute.
An inability to eat or drink safely may require urgent medical care.
Fatigue may be an early sign that depression is developing or returning.
Struggle to get out of bed
Use all available energy at work
Cancel plans because everything feels tiring
A family member may notice that the person is spending more time sitting or lying down, even when sleep does not improve the exhaustion.

Persistent fatigue may also have medical causes. A professional may need to consider anemia, thyroid conditions, sleep disorders, chronic illness, medication effects, pain, or other physical concerns.
Withdrawal from friends, relatives, coworkers, or community activities can be an important warning sign.
Stop attending religious or community activities
Spend most of their time alone
Close the bedroom door for long periods
Say they do not want to burden anyone
Withdrawal may occur because the person feels exhausted, ashamed, emotionally numb, or unable to participate in conversation.
Isolation can increase risk by making it harder for others to notice worsening symptoms.
A sudden or increasing withdrawal is especially concerning when accompanied by hopelessness, substance use, self-neglect, or statements about death.
A noticeable decline in self-care may indicate that depression is becoming more severe.
Wearing the same clothes for several days
These changes should be approached with concern rather than criticism.
The person may care about hygiene but lack the energy, motivation, concentration, or hope needed to complete the task.
A severe decline in self-care may indicate that routine outpatient support is no longer enough.
Depression may begin affecting ordinary responsibilities before the person openly discusses their mood.
Failing to respond to important messages
Becoming unable to care for children or dependents
NIMH includes inability to meet responsibilities or neglect of important roles among behavioral changes associated with depression.
A person does not need to lose all functioning before the change becomes clinically important.
Coworkers, supervisors, or the person themselves may notice:
Statements about being unable to continue
Some people maintain work performance but become unable to function outside work.
They may return home and remain in bed, skip meals, stop communicating, or experience suicidal thoughts.
The ability to remain employed does not rule out severe depression.
Warning Signs at School or College
A student may appear lazy or careless when concentration, sleep, motivation, and hope have been affected.
A sudden decline from the student’s usual performance deserves attention.
Depression may become visible through a decline in home management.
Difficulty maintaining a safe living space
A messy home alone does not diagnose depression.
The concern is the change from the person’s usual functioning, particularly when it occurs alongside low mood, withdrawal, fatigue, sleep changes, or hopelessness.
Depression may affect communication, intimacy, patience, and emotional availability.
Saying the relationship would be better without them
Refusing support because they feel undeserving
Ending relationships abruptly because of hopelessness
Family and partners should avoid treating every relationship difficulty as a symptom.
However, a broad and persistent change across several relationships may indicate worsening depression.
Depression may interfere with the ability to care for children, older adults, or other dependents.
Neglecting personal medication or the dependent person’s medication
Seeking help does not mean someone is an uncaring parent or caregiver.
Additional support may protect both the person with depression and those who depend on them.
Urgent assistance is needed when a dependent person’s essential needs or safety cannot be maintained.
A person may begin using alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, stimulants, or other substances to manage:
Increased alcohol or drug use is also listed among suicide warning signs, particularly when it is new or increasing.
Accurate disclosure supports safer evaluation and treatment.
Risk-Taking or Reduced Concern for Safety
Some people become more withdrawn during depression. Others begin behaving as though their safety does not matter.
Refusing food, medication, or medical care
Saying they do not care what happens
Risk-taking can also occur with mania, substance use, trauma-related conditions, severe agitation, or other concerns.
A sudden increase in dangerous behavior deserves prompt evaluation.
Depression may occur with headaches, digestive concerns, muscle pain, fatigue, and other physical symptoms.
Neglect of an existing health condition
Physical symptoms should not automatically be attributed to depression.
New, severe, or persistent symptoms may require medical assessment.
Warning Signs That Depression Is Returning
People who have experienced depression before may have a recognizable pattern.

SAMHSA recommends identifying personal triggers and warning signs and discussing unusual changes in feelings, thoughts, or behavior with a healthcare professional. Family and friends may also help notice when depression is returning.
A written warning-sign plan may identify:
When an earlier appointment should be requested
When urgent or emergency care is necessary
Children may not describe depression as sadness.
Changes should be evaluated within the child’s developmental level and circumstances.
Ordinary frustration or sadness should not automatically be labeled as depression, but persistent functional or behavioral changes deserve attention.
Statements about having no reason to live should not be dismissed as attention-seeking or drama.
A teenager who suddenly becomes calm after intense distress may still be at risk, particularly if other warning signs are present.
Older adults may show depression through:
Depression is not a normal part of aging.
New symptoms may require review for medical illness, neurological changes, medication effects, pain, grief, isolation, sensory loss, or cognitive disorders.
Sudden confusion or abrupt behavioral change requires medical evaluation.
Warning Signs During Pregnancy or After Childbirth
Depression may develop during pregnancy or after delivery.
Inability to sleep when given the opportunity
A parent can love their baby and still experience significant depression.
Severe confusion, hallucinations, delusions, dangerous behavior, or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby require emergency care.
Warning Signs That May Suggest Bipolar Depression
A depressive episode may occur as part of bipolar disorder.
Tell the evaluating professional about any history of:
Significant activation after starting an antidepressant
A person may seek help during depression and not consider a previous elevated period clinically relevant.
Treatment recommendations may differ when depression occurs as part of bipolar disorder.
Signs That May Point to a Medical Problem
Some apparent depression warning signs may have a medical cause.
Seek medical evaluation when symptoms involve:
Symptoms beginning after a medication change
Thyroid conditions, sleep disorders, infections, neurological illness, medication effects, chronic pain, anemia, hormonal changes, and other medical concerns may resemble or contribute to depression.
Mental and physical health should be considered together.
When Warning Signs Deserve Professional Attention
Consider contacting a healthcare professional when warning signs:
Continue for approximately two weeks or longer
NIMH recommends speaking with a healthcare professional when depression symptoms persist or do not go away.
A person does not need to wait two weeks when symptoms are rapidly worsening, medically dangerous, or affecting safety.
When to Seek Help for Depression.
Urgent evaluation may be needed when someone:
Is rapidly losing the ability to function
Has stopped attending work or school
Is eating or drinking very little
Is using increasing amounts of alcohol or drugs
Suicide warning signs require immediate attention, particularly when the behavior is new, increasing, or connected to a painful event, loss, or major change.
Talking about having no reason to live
Expressing unbearable emotional or physical pain
Obtaining a firearm or stockpiling medication
Making a will or arranging affairs
Suddenly appearing calm after intense distress
NIMH advises getting help as soon as possible when these warning signs appear, especially when the behavior is new or has recently increased.
Passive Thoughts of Death Are Still Important
A person may deny planning suicide but say:
“I wish I would not wake up.”
“It would be easier if I disappeared.”
“I do not care whether I live.”
“My family would be better without me.”
These statements should not be ignored simply because there is no current plan.
Passive thoughts of death may become more active, and professional assessment may be needed.
Directly asking about suicide does not create the idea. It may help the person speak honestly and receive appropriate support.
What to Do When Someone Shows Warning Signs
Approach the person privately and calmly.
“I have noticed that you have stopped answering messages, missed work several times, and said that everyone would be better without you. I am concerned.”
“Do you have access to what you would use?”
Listen without immediately arguing, correcting, or minimizing.
“You have nothing to be depressed about.”
“Promise me you will not tell anyone else.”
Do not promise to keep a suicide plan secret.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone:
May harm themselves or another person
Has a suicide plan and intends to act
Has immediate access to lethal means
Is holding or using a weapon
Is placing children or vulnerable people at risk
If someone says they are going to kill themselves, do not leave them alone and do not promise secrecy. NIMH recommends calling 911 in an immediate life-threatening situation.
In the United States, people experiencing suicidal thoughts or emotional distress may also call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. The service is available 24 hours a day.
The 988 Lifeline does not replace 911 or emergency medical care when there is an attempt, overdose, weapon, severe physical danger, or inability to remain safe.
Do not rely on a routine appointment request, website form, voicemail, email, or patient portal during an immediate emergency.
A person with recurring depression may benefit from documenting their individual warning signs during a period of greater stability.
Signs That I Am Getting Worse
I stay in bed all day
I obtain medication or a weapon
Go to the nearest emergency room
Avoid remaining alone when immediate risk is present
A warning-sign plan should be simple enough to use during a stressful period.
Common Misconceptions About Depression Warning Signs
Some people appear numb, irritable, calm, productive, or socially engaged while experiencing depression.
“Continuing to Work Means the Depression Is Not Serious”
A person may remain employed while experiencing severe hidden impairment or suicidal thoughts.
“Talking About Suicide Is Only a Way to Get Attention”
Suicidal statements should always be taken seriously.
“A Sudden Improvement Means the Risk Has Passed”
A sudden calm period may sometimes occur after someone has made a suicide decision or completed preparations.
“Warning Signs Must Continue for Two Weeks”
The two-week period is relevant to diagnosing certain depressive episodes, but urgent or dangerous warning signs require immediate action.
“Only Mental Health Professionals Can Notice Warning Signs”
Family members, friends, teachers, coworkers, and caregivers may be the first to notice changes.
“Asking About Suicide Will Put the Idea in Someone’s Mind”
Direct, calm questioning can help identify danger and connect the person with support.
A warning sign may have several possible causes. Professional evaluation considers the complete pattern.
How Tinka Health Services Can Help

Tinka Health Services provides psychiatric evaluation, depression assessment, therapy-informed support, medication management when clinically appropriate, and telehealth mental health care for eligible patients in Maryland, Washington, DC, and Virginia.
A depression evaluation may review warning signs involving:

Seliat Dosunmu, DNP, PMHNP-BC, FNP-C, works with patients to understand what has changed, how long the changes have continued, how daily functioning is affected, and whether urgent safety needs are present.
Depending on the clinical evaluation, recommendations may include:
Coordination with therapists or medical professionals
Referral to urgent, emergency, or hospital care when needed

An appointment does not guarantee a depression diagnosis, medication prescription, or specific treatment. Recommendations depend on symptoms, medical history, previous care, functional needs, preferences, and current safety.
Telehealth appointments may be available for eligible patients physically located in Maryland, Washington, DC, or Virginia when virtual care is clinically appropriate.
Tinka Health Services is not an emergency service. For non-emergency psychiatric care, visit
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone may harm themselves or another person, has attempted suicide, has taken an overdose, is experiencing severe psychosis, or cannot remain safe.
Common Signs and Symptoms of Depression
How Depression Can Affect Daily Functioning
When to Seek Help for Depression
Therapy and Practical Support for Depression
Depression warning signs are changes in mood, thinking, behavior, physical health, or daily functioning that may indicate depression is developing, returning, or becoming more severe.

Possible warning signs include loss of interest, increasing hopelessness, irritability, emotional numbness, fatigue, sleep or appetite changes, concentration problems, social withdrawal, declining personal hygiene, missed responsibilities, increased substance use, and reduced concern for personal safety.
The most meaningful warning signs are often changes from the person’s normal behavior. Family members and friends may notice these changes before the person recognizes them.
Persistent or worsening warning signs deserve professional attention. A person does not need to wait until they are completely unable to function.

Statements about wanting to die, feeling like a burden, having no reason to live, developing a suicide plan, giving away belongings, saying goodbye, obtaining lethal means, or showing dangerous behavior require immediate attention.

Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room when someone may act on suicidal thoughts, has attempted suicide, has taken an overdose, is experiencing severe psychosis, cannot meet basic needs, or cannot remain safe.
